name: Renaissance Classical

description.short: The fifteenth- and sixteenth-century Italian recovery of antique proportion, and its conversion by Palladio into a transmissible design method.
description.long:
The Renaissance did not merely imitate Rome; it measured it, theorized it, and then printed it. That last step is the decisive one. Alberti, Serlio, Vignola, and above all Palladio converted a body of ruins into a set of rules a builder in another country and another century could execute from a plate.

The Quattro Libri of 1570 is the direct ancestor of the pattern book, the plan book, and the parametric catalog. Anyone building a rules-based design system today is working in a tradition that begins here, and would do well to notice both what it achieved and where it went thin — Palladio's rules govern proportion beautifully and say almost nothing about how a house grows.

defining_characteristics: Antique proportion recovered by measurement rather than inherited by craft
The treatise as the primary medium of transmission
Harmonic and geometric room ratios governing plan as well as elevation
The villa as a complete diagram of dwelling, agriculture, and status
